ROBERTSON,  Hon.  Thomas,  judge 
and  jurist,  is  the  eld.  s.  of  the  late 
Alex.  Robertson,  Goderich,  Ont.,  by 
his  wife,  Matilda,  eld.  dau.  of  Col. 
T.  G.  Simons,  who  was  wounded, 
losing  his  right  arm  at  the  battle 
of  Lundy’s  Lane,  and  was  Sheriff  of 
the  old  Gore  Dist.  His  Lordship  is 
descended  from  the  Robertsons  of 
Struan,  chiefs  of  Clan  Donnachie. 
B.  at  Ancaster,  Ont.,  Jan.  25,  1827, 


he  was  ed.  at  the  London  and  Huron 
Dist.  Grammar  schs.  and  at  the 
Univ.  of  Toronto.  He  studied  law 
with  the  late  Hon.  J.  H.  Cameron, 
Q.C. ,  was  admitted  an  atty. ,  1849, 
and  called  to  the  bar,  1852.  Created 
a  Q.C.,  by  the  Earl  of  Dufferin,  1873, 
he  became  a  Bencher  of  the  Law 
Soc.,  1874.  He  commenced  the 
practice  of  his  profession  at  Dun- 
das,  but  soon  removed  to  Hamilton, 
where  he  established  an  extensive 
and  successful  business.  He  was 
the  first  Crown  Atty.  for  Went¬ 
worth.  A  Con.  in  politics,  he  ran  in 
that  interest  for  the  representation 
of  South  Wentworth  in  the  Ho.  of 
Commons,  at  the  g.  e.  1867,  and  was 
defeated  by  27  votes.  He  was  re¬ 
turned  for  Hamilton  at  the  g.  e. 
1878,  and  throughout  his  Parliament¬ 
ary  career,  warmly  supported  the 
late  Sir  John  Macdonald,  more  espe¬ 
cially  in  connection  with  the  N.  P. , 
of  which  he  was  a  staunch  advocate 
as  far  back  as  1867.  He  was  ele¬ 
vated  to  the  bench  as  a  Justice  of 
the  High  Ct.  of  Justice,  Ont.,  Chan¬ 
cery  Div.,  Feb.  11,  1887.  His  Lord- 
ship  is  a  mem.  of  the  Ang.  Ch. ,  and 
m.  June,  1850,  Frances  Louisa, 
young,  dau.  of  the  late  Theodore 
Reed,  one  of  the  earliest  pioneers  of 
the  “  Huron  Tract.”  Their  s.,  Fran¬ 
cis  Beverley  R.  (now  practising  law 
in  Winnipeg,  Man.),  won  the  Gil¬ 
christ  scholarship,  1870. — “Bannoch 
Lodge,”  Hamilton;  Osgoode  Hall, 
Toronto.

been  V.-P.  of  the  Math.  Assn,  of 
Ont.,  and  is  now  V.-P.  of  the 
Y.M.C.A.  of  Ont.  and  Quebec.  In

Free  Library  Bd.  Politically,  Mr.  R. 
is  an  Ind.  Lib.  He  believes  in  Free 
Trade  as  far  as  it  can  be  obtained ; 
the  political  Ind.  of  Can. ;  unsectar¬ 
ian  schs. ;  the  development  of  a  Can. 
sentiment  and  literature  ;  and  the 
moderation  of  party  feeling.  He 
m.  1887,  Margt.  K.,  young,  dau.  of 
John  Junkin,  St.  Catharines. — St. 
Catharines,  Ont.

the  9th  Internl.  Med.  Congress,  held 
at  Washington,  1877.  As  an  origi¬ 
nal  investigator  in  the  field  of 
dermat.  enquiry,  his  writings  have 
been  numerous  and  are  everywhere 
highly  regarded  by  the  med.  profes¬ 
sion.  His  best  known  work  is  “A 
Manual  of  Dermat.”  (N.  Y. ,  1886). 
In  1895  he  wrote  on  a  hitherto  un¬ 
described  disease  of  the  skin,  and 
called  it  “  hidrocystoriia.”  At  pres¬ 
ent  (1898)  he  is  writing  on  “  Cancer 
of  the  Skin.”  Dr.  R.  devotes  him¬ 
self  exclusively  to  science,  and  has 
no  time  for  politics.  He  is,  however, 
of  the  opinion  that  Can.  and  the 
U.  S.  should  be  politically  united. 
He  was  brought  up  a  Presb. ,  but  he 
respects  all  religions  that  teach 
morality,  and  “to  do  unto  others 
as  you  would  that  they  should  do 
unto  you.”  He  m.  1878,  Miss 
Marie  Kress,  Vienna,  Austria. — S/fS 
West  4%nd  St.,  New  York. 

“  His  name  sufficient  to  call  attention 
to  any  work  on  dermat.  of  which  he  is  the 
author.” — Brit.  Med.  Journal. 

ROBINSON,  Miss  Augusta  Louisa, 

vocalist,  is  the  young,  dau.  of  the 
late  Hon.  John  Beverley  Robinson, 
Lt. -Gov.  of  Ont. ,  1880-87,  by  his 
wife,  Mary  Jane,  dau.  of  the  late 
H  on.  C.  A.  Hagerman,  a  Justice  of 
the  Queen’s  Bench,  U.  C.  B.  in 
Toronto,  she  received  her  early 
musical  education  in  her  native  city, 
continuing  it  under  Agramonte,  in 
N.  Y.  She  then  spent  a  year  in 
Paris,  under  Mad.  La  Borde,  and 
worked  hard  for  3  yrs.  in  London, 
gaining  experience  under  Randegger 
and  Henschel.  While  in  Eng. ,  she 
made  a  tour  in  the  provinces  with 
Maud  Valerie  White  (some  of  whose 
songs  she  sings),  Plunkett  Green 
and  others.  Returning  to  Can., 


1895,  she  achieved  great  success  in 
the  “Creation,”  and  also  whilst 
abroad,  in  “  Elijah”  and  the  “  Mes¬ 
siah.”  In  Dec.,  1896,  she  accom¬ 
panied  Mad.  Albani  on  an  extended 
tour  in  Can.  and  the  U.  S. ,  as  her 
chief  support.  Her  voice  is  a  so¬ 
prano  of  mezzo  quality,  well  suited 
to  the  just  interpretation  of  great 
oratorio  works.  She  inherits  her 
musical  gifts  from  her  mother,  who 
was  a  talented  amateur  vocalist. — 
10  Ros/t  St.,  Toronto. 

“A  voice  clear  and  true  as  a  bell.” — 
Province. 

ROBINSON,  Maj.-Genl.  Charles 
Walker,  Lieut. -Governor  and  Secy, 
of  Chelsea  Hospital,  is  the  4th  and 
young,  s.  of  the  late  Chief-Justice 
Sir  J.  B.  Robinson,  Bart.  (U.  E.  L. 
descent).  He  was  b.  at  Beverley 
House,  Toronto,  Apl.  3,  1836,  and 
received  his  education  at  U.  C. 
Coll,  and  Trinity  Univ.,  Toronto, 
where  he  took  his  degree  in  1855, 
being  made  a  D.C.L.  (hon.  causd ) 
of  the  same,  1879.  Though  orig¬ 
inally  intended  for  the  army,  he 
had  about  determined  to  adopt 
another  career  when  circumstances 
combined  to  confirm  his  original  in¬ 
tention.  Can.  had  contributed  gen¬ 
erously  to  the  Patriotic  Fund  during 
the  Crimean  war,  and  H.  R.  H.  the 
Prince  Consort  was  desirous  of  ac¬ 
knowledging  it  by  bestowing  a  com¬ 
mission  in  his  own  distinguished 
regt. ,  the  Rifle  Brigade,  upon  some 
worthy  Can.  For  many  yrs.  both 
the  public  and  private  life  of  U.  C. 
had  been  dignified  and  adorned  by 
Sir  J.  B.  Robinson,  who,  alike  by 
official  station  and  public  consent, 
was  regarded  as  the  most  eminent 
subject  of  the  Crown  in  his  province. 
It  was,  therefore,  a  fitting  and  grace¬ 
ful  acknowledgment  of  his  un¬ 
doubted  pre-eminence  that  this  com¬ 
mission  should  have  been  placed  at 
the  disposal  of  one  of  the  mems.  of 
his  family,  without  purchase,  and 
such  having  been  done,  his  young, 
s.,  under  circumstances  gratifying 
to  the  whole  community,  began  a 
career  which  has  been  watched  with 
interest  by  all  Canadians.  Entering 


872 


ROBINSON. 


the  service  in  1857  as  2nd  lieut.  in 
the  Rifle  Brigade,  he  remained  in 
that  corps  until  1885.  He  served 
with  the  2nd  Batt.  of  his  regt.  dur¬ 
ing  the  Indian  mutiny  (medal),  and 
throughout  the  second  phase  of  the 
Ashanti  war,  from  Dec.  12,  1873, 
as  Brigade  Major  to  the  European 
Brigade,  including  the  battle  of 
Amoaful,  battle  of  Ordahsu,  and 
capture  of  Coomassie  (mentioned  in 
despatches,  Bt.  of  Major,  medal 
with  clasp).  He  served  in  the  Zulu 
war,  1879,  and  was  present  in  the 
engagement  at  Ulundi  (mentioned 
in  despatches,  Bt.  of  Lt.  -Col. ,  medal 
with  clasp).  He  became  a  full  col., 
1885,  and  went  on  half-pay  in  the 
following  year.  His  merits  have 
been  recognized  by  the  many  im¬ 
portant  staff  appts.  which  he  has 
held.  He  was  for  a  time  Mil.  In¬ 
structor  at  Sandhurst,  then  Asst. 
Adjt.-Genl.  at  Aldershot,  and  Bri¬ 
gade  Major  there.  In  1890  he  be¬ 
came  Asst.  Mil.  Secy,  at  the  Horse 
Guards.  In  1892  he  was  apptd.  to 
the  command  of  the  troops  at  the 
Mauritius,  carrying  with  it  the  tem¬ 
porary  rank  of  Maj.  -Genl.,  an  appt. 
all  the  more  popular  in  the  ser¬ 
vice,  as  it  saved  Col.  R.  from  the 
operation  of  the  57  yrs.  rule,  to 
which  he  would  have  fallen  a  victim 
under  other  circumstances.  The 
Army  and  Navy  Gazette,  in  a  highly 
eulogistic  article,  expressed  the  satis¬ 
faction  which  was  felt  in  the  service 
that  an  officer,  “zealous,  courteous, 
capable  and  deserving,”  should  thus 
escape  a  regulation  which  had  been 
disastrous  to  the  hopes  and  aspira¬ 
tions  of  so  many  old  and  deserving 
officers,  and  declared  that  the  whole 
service  would  regard  it  as  a  healthy 
sign  of  the  encouragement  of  merit. 
He  returned  to  Eng.  early  in  1895 
to  assume  the  duties  of  Lt.-Gov.  and 
Secy,  of  Chelsea  Hospital,  which 
post  he  still  retains.  He  is  the 
author  of  a  small  vol. :  “Obser¬ 
vations  on  the  Battle  of  Sedan  ” 
(1871),  and  has  translated  a  book  by 
the  Duke  of  Wurtemberg  on  the 
system  of  attack  of  the  Prussian 
Infy.  in  the  campaign  of  1870-71. 


He  was  apptd.  a  C.B.,  1887,  and  was 
awarded  a  distinguished  service  pen¬ 
sion,  1896.  Gen.  R.  m.  1884,  Margt. 
Frances,  eld.  dau.  of  Genl.  Sir 
Archibald  Alison,  G.  C.  B. — Royal 
Hospital,  Chelsea,  London,  Eng.; 
Army  and  Navy  Club. 

ROBINSON,  Christopher,  Q.C.,  is 
the  3rd  s.  of  the  late  Hon.  Sir  J.  B. 
Robinson,  C.B.,  and  was  b.  at  Bev¬ 
erley  House,  Toronto,  Jan.  21,  1828. 
He  was  ed.  at  U.  C.  Coll,  and  King’s 
Coll.,  Toronto,  afterwards  taking  an 
ad  eund.  degree  at  Trinity  Univ. , 
Toronto.  He  was  called  to  the  bar, 
1850,  beginning  the  practice  of  his 
profession  in  1852,  the  two  inter¬ 
vening  yrs.  having  been  spent  in 
travel.  Mr.  R.  was  apptd.  Reporter 
to  the  Ct.  of  Queen’s  Bench,  1856, 
and  continued  as  such  until  1872, 
when  the  system  being  changed  and 
assimilated  to  that  of  Eng. ,  he  be¬ 
came  ed.  of  the  “Law  Reports.’ 
In  1885  he  was  elected  a  Bencher  of 
the  Law  Soc.  of  U.  C.,  and  retired 
from  the  editorship  of  the  “  Re¬ 
ports.”  For  many  yrs.  he  travelled 
the  western  circuit,  only  accepting 
special  retainers  elsewhere.  De¬ 
voting  himself  exclusively  to  his 
profession  he  has  been  engaged  in 
many  cases  of  great  public  interest 
and  importance,  notably  the  case  of 
Whelan,  convicted  in  1868  of  the 
murder  of  the  Hon.  T.  D.  McGee, 
M.P.,  when  he  argued  for  the  Crown 
the  writ  of  error  after  the  trial 
(28  U.  C.  R.  1).  He  appeared  for 
the  defence  in  the  famous  political 
libel  suit  of  the  Queen  vs.  Wilkin¬ 
son,  and  made  the  application  to  the 
Court  to  have  the  late  Hon.  Geo. 
Brown  convicted  for  contempt  for 
his  attack  on  the  late  Sir  Adam 
Wilson  (41  U.  C.  R.  1).  In  1884  he 
argued  before  the  Judicial  Comte,  of 
the  Privy  Council  the  case  for  the 
Dom.  Govt,  in  the  arbitration  with 
the  Province  of  Man.,  respecting 
the  boundaries  of  that  province. 
In  1885  he  was  leading  counsel  for 
the  Crown  in  the  prosecution  of 
Louis  Riel,  at  Regina,  for  high  trea¬ 
son,  and,  in  1889-90,  he  represented 
the  Dom.  Govt,  in  the  arbitration

with  the  Can.  Pac.  Ry.,  arising  out 
of  the  construction  of  that  road.  In

the  U.  S.,  the  arbitrators  being 
Lord  Hannen  and  the  late  Sir  John 
Thompson,  selected  by  Gt.  Brit. ; 
Judge  Harlan  of  the  Supreme  Ct. , 
and  Senator  Morgan,  for  the  U.  S. ; 
the  Baron  de  Courcel  ( Presdt.  of  the 
Tribunal),  now  French  Ambassador 
in  London,  apptd.  by  the  French 
Govt. ;  Mr.  Gram,  by  the  Govt,  of 
Sweden,  and  Viscount  Venesta,  by 
that  of  Italy ;  and  was  specially 
complimented  by  the  London  Times 
for  the  “brilliant  speech  at  the  con¬ 
clusion  of  the  argument  in  which  he 
summarized  the  whole  case,  reduc¬ 
ing  it  to  a  series  of  concise  proposi¬ 
tions  which,  from  the  Brit,  point  of 
view,  demonstrated  the  absurdity  of 
the  Am.  claims.”  Upon  the  conclu¬ 
sion  of  his  labours  before  this  tri¬ 
bunal,  Mr.  R.  was  ottered  knight¬ 
hood  for  his  services,  which  for  pri¬ 
vate  reasons  he  respectfully  declined. 
Except  in  so  far  as  the  duties  of  his 
profession  are  concerned,  Mr.  R.  is 
in  no  way  connected  with  public 
life,  and  is  in  no  sense  a  public 
man.  It  is  well  known  that  he  has 
frequently  been  pressed  by  Govt, 
to  accept  of  judicial  appts.,  upon 
vacancies  arising  in  various  cts. ,  but 
he  has  steadily  declined  the  highest 
preferment.  He  is  the  acknowledged 
leader  of  the  bar  of  Ont.,  and  before 


the  Supreme  Ct.  and  the  Privy 
Council,  is  recognized  as  leader  of 
the  Can.  bar.  A  mem.  of  the  Ang. 
Ch.,  he  m.  July  2,  1879,  Elizabeth 
Street,  eld.  dau.  of  the  late  Hon. 
J.  B.  Plumb,  Speaker  of  the  Senate  of 
Can.—  “  Beverley  House”  Toronto; 
Toronto  Club  ;  Rideau  Club ,  Ottawa. 

“There  is  no  member  of  the  Can.  bar 
worthier  of  distinction  on  the  ground  of 
ability,  legal  learning,  or  the  possession  of 
those  rarer  qualities  of  head  and  heart  which 
find  no  better  name  than  the  good  old  term, 
gentleman.” — Week. 

ROBINSON,  Christopher  Blackett, 

editor  and  publisher,  was  b.  in  Tho- 
rah,  Ont.,  1837.  Ed.  there,  he 
entered  journalism  at  20,  becoming 
ed.  of  the  Beaverton  Post.  Remov¬ 
ing  to  Lindsay,  1801,  he  continued 
the  publication  of  his  paper  in  that 
town  for  10  yrs.  Disposing  of  the 
Post,  he  removed  to  Toronto,  where 
he  began  the  publication  of  the  Can. 
Presbyterian.  This  influential  jour¬ 
nal  became  amalgamated  with  the 
Westminster,  1897,  under  a  co.  of 
which  Mr.  R.  was  apptd.  Presdt. — 
the  outcome  being  a  weekly  religious 
paper,  unique  in  Can.  journalism, 
presenting  all  the  strong  points  of  a 
weekly  newspaper  and  a  monthly 
mag.  Mr.  R.,  in  addition  to  his 
other  work,  was  for  many  yrs.  pub¬ 
lisher  and  mangr.  of  the  Week,  and 
became  ed.  of  that  paper,  1 896.  He 
is  an  adherent  of  the  Presb.  Ch., 
and  m.  the  dau.  of  the  late  Wm. 
Cameron,  London,  Ont.  —  70  St. 
Alban  St..,  Toronto.

ROBINSON,  Rev.  George  Livingstone 

(Presb. ),  educationist,  was  b.  at  West 
Hebron,  N.Y.,  Aug.  19,  1864.  After 
graduating  at  Princeton  Coll. ,  N.  J. , 
1887,  he  spent  3  yrs.  at  Beyrout, 
Syria,  as  an  instructor  in  the  Syrian 
Prot.  Coll,  at  that  place,  and  there 
conceived  a  special  taste  for  Oriental 
studies.  This  was  deepened  during 
his  theol.  course  at  Princeton  Semy., 
1890-93.  During  the  vacations  he 
attended  the  summer  sch.  at  Chau¬ 
tauqua  and  elsewhere,  under  the 
direction  of  Dr.  Harper,  in  order 
to  perfect  himself  yet  more  in 
these  studies.  Upon  graduating 
from  Princeton  Theol.  Semy.,  he 
was  awarded  the  Fellowship  in 
Old  Test,  literature,  which  carries 
with  it  an  income  of  $600  and  the 
privilege  of  spending  a  year  at  a 
foreign  univ.  in  Old  Test,  study. 
This  was  continued  to  him  for  a 
second  year,  a  favour  which  has 
been  accorded  to  only  one  other 
person.  He  prosecuted  his  studies 
for  one  year  at  the  Univ.  of  Berlin, 
and  for  one  year  at  Leipsie  (Ph.D. , 
1895).  The  thesis  he  presented  on 
this  occasion  was  a  defence  of  the 
unity  of  the  Book  of  Zechariah, 
which  has  been  reprinted.  He  m. 
Miss  Jessie  Patten  Lee  Harvey,  of 
Cairo,  Egypt,  before  coming  home. 
On  his  return  from  Germany,  he 
became  pastor  of  Roxbury  Presb. 
Ch.,  Boston,  and  he  was  still  fulfil¬ 
ling  the  duties  of  that  position  when 
apptd.  (June,  1896)  to  that  which 
he  at  present  holds,  viz.,  the  pro¬ 
fessorship  of  Old  Test.  Lit.  in  Knox 
Coll. ,  Toronto.  ^  He  delivered  his 
inaugural  lecture,  Oct.  7,  1896, 
taking  for  his  subject:  “The  Place 
of  Deuteronomy  in  Hebrew  Litera¬ 
ture.” — 619  Spadina  Are.,  Toronto.

service,  is  a  native  of  the  Province 


of  N.  B.  In  1893  he  was  apptd.

of  the  great  Empire  of  Can.  ”  He  m. 
July,  1882,  Miss  Lillian  Isabel  Lynes, 
of  Auburn,  N.  Y. — 845  Boyleston  St., 
Boston,  Mass. ;  Universalist  Club, 
do.;  Boston  Art  Club,  do.;  20th  Cen¬

ROE,  The  Venerable  Henry,  Arch¬ 
deacon  of  Quebec  (Ch.  of  Eng.),  is 
the  s.  of  the  late  John  Hill  Roe, 

M. D.,  T.C.D.,  St.  John’s,  P.Q.,  by 
his  wife,  Jane  Ardagh,  both  belonging 
to  very  old  Irish  families.  B.  at 
Henry ville,  P.Q.,  Feb.  22,  1829,  he 
was  ed.  at  first  in  Workman’s  Sch., 
and  afterwards  at  Archdeacon  Scott’s 
Sch.,  both  in  Montreal.  Entering 
McGill  Univ.,  1843,  as  Longueuil 
scholar,  he  migrated  to  Bishop’s 
Coll.,  Lennoxville,  on  its  being 


established,  1845  (B.A.,  and  Mackie 
prizeman,  1855  ;  M.A. ,  1867  ;  B.D., 
1879;  D.D.,  1879;  lion.  D.C.L., 
1896).  Ordained  deacon,  1852,  and 
priest,  1853,  by  the  late  Bp.  Moun¬ 
tain,  he  went  first  as  mission,  to 
New  Ireland.  In  1855  he  was  apptd. 
incumbent  of  St.  Matthew’s,  Quebec, 
and  was  apptd.  examg.  chaplain  to 
the  Lord  Bp.  of  the  Diocese,  1865. 
Resigning  his  city  appt. ,  1868,  to 
throw  himself  into  mission,  work,  he 
accepted  charge  of  Richmond  and 
Melbourne  in  the  E.  T. ,  which,  under 
his  hands,  grew  into  a  rectory.  From 
this  position  he  was  called,  1873,  to 
take  the  chair  of  Divinity  and  Pas¬ 
toral  Tlieol.  in  his  Alma  Mater. 
Later,  he  became  Dean  of  this 
Faculty,  and  Vice-Principal  of  the 
Coll.,  1882.  In  1884,  through  his 
untiring  efforts,  $25,000  were  raised 
towards  the  Harrold  Divinity  Fund 
of  the  Coll.,  and  also  endowments 
were  established  for  the  Principal’s 
chair,  and  the  chair  of  Pastoral 
Theol.  Dr.  R.  was  apptd.  Arch¬ 
deacon  of  Quebec,  1888,  being  next 
in  succession  (after  an  interval  of 
25  yrs.)  to  the  revered  Bp.  G.  J. 
Mountain.  In  1891  he  retired  from 
Bishop’s  Coll.,  and  accepted  the 
appt.  of  Genl.  Mission.  Agent  of  the 
Diocese.  This  he  resigned,  1894. 
He  then  accepted  his  present  charge, 
the  mission  of  Brompton  and  Wind¬ 
sor.  In  1873  he  was  one  of  5  clergy¬ 
men  who  were  nominated  by  the 
Ho.  of  Bishops  for  the  Bishopric 
of  Algoma.  He  has  been  a  del. 
to  both  the  Provl.  and  the  Genl. 
synods  from  their  establishment, 
and  has  been  also  on  the  comte. 
apptd.  by  the  former  to  consider  the 
question  how  best  to  restore  the 
unity  of  the  Church.  During  Bp. 
Williams’s  absence  from  the  diocese 
for  a  year,  in  1888,  and  on  some 
occasions  since,  Archdeacon  R.  ad¬ 
ministered  the  Diocese  as  Commis¬ 
sary  and  V. -G.  As  such  also  he 
presided  at  the  Synod  which  resulted 
in  the  election  of  Bp.  Dunn.  He  was 
apptd.  by  Archbp.  Lewis  to  preach 
before  the  Provl.  Synod,  1895.  He 
is  regarded  in  all  quarters  as  a

ROGERS,  Lt.-Col.  Robert  Zaccheus, 
V.  M.,  bro.  of  H.  C.  Rogers  (q.v.), 
was  b.  at  Grafton,  Ont.,  Mch.  29, 
1842,  and  ed.  at  U.  C.  Coll.  A 
farmer  and  mill-owner,  he  has  also 
long  been  conspicuous  among  his 
class  and  friends  for  his  devotion  to 
the  interests  of  the  V.  M.  Taking 
a  1st  class  Infy.  cert,  at  the  M.  S., 
he  raised  and  was  apptd.  capt.  of 
No.  1  Co.,  40th  Batt.,  Aug.,  1866, 
with  which  he  assisted  in  repelling 
the  Fenians  at  that  time.  Having 
received  theBt.  of  Maj.,  Aug.,  1871, 
he  was  promoted  Lt.-Col.,  Mch., 
1885,  and  remains  in  command  of 
the  batt.  In  1880  he  organized  a  co. 
to  colonize  and  develop  the  Souris 
River  Valley,  N,W.T. ,  and  he  be¬ 
came  the  pioneer  mill-owner  and 
settler  in  that  region.  The  enter¬ 
prise  did  not  result  successfully, 
and  Col.  R.  reluctantly  abandoned 
the  idea  of  establishing  his  future 
home  in  the  valley  He  is  the  author 
of  “Incidents  in  the  Early  Military 
History  of  Can.”  (“Trans.  Can.  Mil. 


Inst.,  1890-91).  In  politics,  he  is 
strongly  Con. — Grafton,  Ont.

ROSAMOND,  Bennett,  manufac¬ 
turer  and  legislator,  is  the  s.  of  the 
late  James  Rosamond,  a  native  of 
Leitrim,  Irel.,  by  his  wife,  Margt. 
Wilson,  a  native  of  Paisley,  Scot. 
B.  at  Carleton  Place,  Ont. ,  May  10, 
1833,  he  was  ed.  at  the  Grammar 
Sch.  there,  and  commenced  his 
business  career  under  his  father, 
who  had  established  flour,  woollen 
and  others  mills  at  that  village.  In 
1857  the  family  moved  to  Almonte, 
the  father  having  purchased  the 
ground  property  and  rights  of  the 
Ramsay  Woollen  Cloth  Manfy.,  and 
built  mills  there.  In  1862  he  and 
his  bro.  Wm.  took  a  lease  of  the 
concern.  They  doubled  the  capacity 
of  their  mill,  and,  in  1866,  admitted 
George  Stephen  (now  Lord  Mount 
Stephen)  as  a  partner.  Since  then 
the  business  has  continued  to  grow, 
and  is  now  known  as  the  Rosamond 
Woollen  Co.,  Mr.  R.  being  Presdt. 
thereof.  He  is  also  Presdt.  of  the 
Almonte  Knitting  Co.,  and  is  inter¬ 
ested  in  the  Cobourg  Woollen  Co., 
of  which  his  bro.  is  Presdt.  In 
1890  he  was  elected  Presdt.  of  the 
Can.  Mantra’.  Assn.  As  a  public 
man,  he  was  Reeve  and  afterwards 
Mayor  of  Almonte  and  Chairman  of 
the  Bd.  of  Education.  Politically,  a 
Con.,  he  unsuccessfully  contested 
North  Lanark  for  the  Ho.  of  Com¬ 
mons,  as  an  Ind.  member  of  the 
party,  against  Hon.  Wm.  Macdou- 
gall,  Nov.,  1864,  and  was  again  a  can¬ 
didate  for  the  same  seat,  g.  e.  1872. 
He  was  also  unsuccessful  at  the 
Provl.  g.  e.  1871.  He  was  first 
returned  to  the  Ho.  of  Commons, 
Dec.,  1891,  replacing  Mr.  Jamieson, 
on  his  appt.  as  a  Co.  Ct.  Judge,  and 
has  been  re-elected  at  every  subse¬ 
quent  appeal  to  the  people.  He 
was  apptd.  a  mem.  of  the  Finance 


Comte,  of  the  Lib. -Con.  Union  of 
Ont.,  1896.  He  is  a  believer  in  a 
moderate  protective  policy,  and 
favours  reciprocity  with  the  U.  S. 
so  far  as  possible,  consistent  with 
our  connection  with  Eng.  He  is 
totally  opposed  to  anything  likely 
to  bring  about  annexation  to  the 
U.  S.  He  is  a  mem.  of  the  Ch.  of 
Eng.,  and  m.  Miss  Adair  M.  Roy 
(she  d.  Dec.,  1897). — Almonte ,  Ont.; 
Rideau  Club;  St.  James’s  Club. 

“  A  man  of  great  executive  ability,  large 
business  experience,  and  knowledge  of  pub¬ 
lic  affairs.” — G.  M.  Adam. 

ROSE,  Charles  Day,  hanker,  is  the

Ry.,  and  remained  a  mem.  of  the

Eng.  turf,  including  a  2000  guinea 
race  at  Newmarket,  1886.  In  1893  he

but  was  subsequently  withdrawn  by 
Mr.  R.  in  view  of  “  the  general  im¬

opinion  on  the  result  of  the  last

ROSE,  George  MacLean,  author  and 
publisher,  was  b.  in  Wick,  Caith- 
ness-shire,  Scot.,  Mch.  14,  1829, 
and  learned  the  art  of  printing 
in  the  office  of  the  John  o’ Groat 
Journal.  Coming  to  Can.  when  a 
young  man,  he  established  a  job 
office  in  Montreal,  proceeding  after¬ 
wards  to  Merrickville,  Ont.,  where 
he  became  connected  with  the  Mer¬ 
rickville  Chronicle,  a  weekly  paper 
founded  by  the  Rev.  Dr.  Muir  (q.  v. ). 
Subsequently,  he  was  city  ed.  of  the 
London  Prototype,  under  the  late 
Marcus  Talbot,  M.P.  In  1858  he 
became  mangr.  for  the  late  Sami. 
Thompson,  Toronto,  for  whom  he 
published  the  Daily  Atlas,  and  with 
whom  he  went  to  Quebec,  1859,  on 
the  latter’s  becoming  Parliamentary 
and  Department  Printer  there.  Mr. 
R.  remained  with  Mr.  T.  until  he 
threw  up  his  contract  in  the  early 
sixties.  A  new  firm  was  then 
formed — the  firm  of  Hunter,  Rose 
&  Co. — which  took  over  the  contract 
and  secured  its  renewal.  When  the 
seat  of  govt,  was  transferred  to 
Ottawa,  1865,  Hunter,  Rose  k  Co.

went,  with  it,  and  from  that  time,

books.  For  this  purpose  they 
opened  a  branch  in  Toronto,  to 
which  city  the  firm  removed  its 
entire  establishment  on  the  termin¬ 
ation  of  their  contract  with  the 
Dom.  Govt.,  1871.  They  had  pre¬ 
viously  obtained  a  10  years’  contract 
for  the  printing  required  by  the 
Provl.  Govt.  They  now  entered 
extensively  into  the  business  of

popular  novels  of  living  writers,  for 
which  a  ready  market  was  found. 
They  also  published  latterly  at  their 
own  risk  the  Can.  Monthly  and  the 
Rose-Belford  Mag.  Mr.  R.  is  now 
the  “Nestor”  of  his  profession  in 
Can. ,  and  it  is  satisfactory  to  know 
that  his  industry  and  enterprise 
have  placed  him  in  a  position  of 
pecuniary  ind.  Widely  as  he  is

long  total  abstainer  and  prohibi¬

various  organizations.  He  has  at¬ 
tained  the  highest  offices  in  the  gift

having  been  chosen  several  times  to 
fill  the  chair  of  Grand  Worthy  Pa¬ 
triarch  of  the  order,  both  in  Quebec 
and  Ont. ,  and  he  has  likewise  held 
the  second  highest  position  attain¬ 
able  in  the  order  on  this  continent — 
that  of  Most  Worthy  Associate  of 
the  National  Div.  of  North  Am. 
Mr.  R.  was  one  of  the  founders  of 
the  Presb.  Ladies’  Coll. ,  Ottawa,  and 
was  the  chief  promoter  of  the  Temp. 
Colonization  Co.,  1882.  He  is  now 
a  dir.  of  the  Ontario  Bank.  He  was 
formerly  Treas.  of  the  Toronto  Bd. 
of  Trade,  and  became  Presdt.  of 
that  body,  1882.  He  has  been  also 
Presdt.  of  the  Caithness  Club,  To¬ 
ronto.  He  has  compiled  several 
useful  books  of  reference,  and  has

of  Practice  under  the  J.  Act,  Ont. 
Politically,  he  was  formerly  a  Con.

of  more  than  ordinary  interest,  in¬ 
cluding  Reg.  vs.  Connolly  &  Mc- 
Greevy,  and  what  are  known  as  the

and  the  verdict  given  Apl.  24  follow¬

ROSS,  Alexander  Milton,  M.D., 

philanthropist  and  scientist,  was  b. 
at  Belleville,  Ont.,  Dec.  13,  1832. 
He  is  the  s.  of  Win.  Ross,  by  his 
wife,  Frederika  Grant,  who  were  de¬ 
scendants  of  Scottish  Highlanders, 
who  came  to  Can.  from  Ross-shire, 
Scot.,  1785.  Early  in  life  he  evinced 
a  groat  love  for  natural  history. 
He  attended  a  soli,  at  Belleville  till 
his  lltli  year,  when  the  death  of  his 
father  compelled  him  to  seek  em¬ 
ployment.  Proceeding  to  N.  Y.  he 
became  a  compositor  on  the  Evening 
Rost.  The  ed.  of  the  paper  was 
Wm.  Cullen  Bryant,  the  poet,  who 
became  interested  in  the  boy  and 
remained  his  friend  in  after  life. 
During  this  period  lie  became  ac¬ 
quainted  with  Garibaldi,  who  was 
then  a  rosidont  of  N.  Y. ,  and,  in 
1874,  Dr.  R.  was  instrumental  in 
securing  a  pension  for  the  patriot 
from  the  Italian  Govt.  Studying 
mod.  under  Dr.  Valentine  Mott,  he 
received  his  degree,  1855,  and  was 
afterwards  admitted  a  mem.  of  the 
Coll,  of  Pliys.  and  Surgs.,  both  in 


884 


ROSS. 


Ont.  and  Quebec.  Soon  after  grad¬ 
uation  he  was  apptd.  a  surg.  in  the 
Nicaraguan  army  under  Walker. 
In  1850  he  became  actively  engaged 
in  the  anti-slavery  struggle  in  the 
U.  S. ,  and  was  a  personal  friend  and 
co-worker  of  John  Brown,  of  Osawa- 
tomie.  Of  his  efforts  in  this  cause 
Mr.  Gladstone  has  said  :  “No  one  can 
deny  the  skill,  forethought  and 
tenacity  which  you  exhibited,  or 
withhold  his  admiration  for  the 
signal  courage,  disinterestedness  and 
humanity  which  formed  the  basis  of 
your  whole  proceedings;”  During 
the  Am.  civil  war  he  served  for  a 
short  time  as  a  surg.  in  the  Federal 
army,  and  was  afterwards  employed 
by  Presdt.  Lincoln  on  a  confidential 
mission  in  Can.  He  subsequently 
offered  his  services  to  Presdt.  Juarez, 
of  Mexico,  and  received  the  appt. 
of  surg.  in  the  Mexican  army. 
After  the  overthrow  of  the  Empire 
he  returned  to  Can.,  where  he  de¬ 
voted  himself  to  the  collection  and 
classification  of  the  fauna  and  flora 
of  his  native  country,  a  work 
that  had  never  before  been  at¬ 
tempted  by  a  native  Can.  He  has 
collected  and  classified  hundreds  of 
species  of  birds,  eggs,  mammals, 
reptiles  and  fresh  water  fishes,  3400 
species  of  insects,  and  2000  species 
of  Can.  flora.  He  was  apptd.  an 
Offi-cier  de  V Acad.  Frangais,  1878  ; 
and  became  a  Fellow  of  the  Royal 
Acad,  of  Science,  Italy,  1879.  He 
has  also  received  the  honour  of 
knighthood  from  the  Emperor  of 
Russia  and  from  other  crowned 
heads.  Among  his  various  publica¬ 
tions  Appleton  mentions  the  follow¬ 
ing  :  “Recollections  of  an  Aboli¬ 
tionist”  (1867);  “Birds  of  Can.” 
(1872);  “Butterflies  and  Moths  of 
Can.”  (1873);  “  Flora  of  Can.  ”  (do.); 
“Forest  Trees  of  Can.”  (1874); 
“  Ferns  and  Wild  Flowers  of  Can.” 
(1877);  “Mammals,  Reptiles  and 
FreshWater  Fishes  of  Can.”  (1878)  ; 
“  Vaccination  a  Medical  Delusion” 
(1885),  and  “Med.  Practice  of  the 
Future”  (1887).  During  the  small¬ 
pox  epidemic  in  Montreal,  18S5,  Dr. 
R.  was  a  prominent  opponent  of 


vaccination,  declaring  that  it  was 
not  only  useless  as  a  preventative  of 
small  pox,  but  that  it  propagated  the 
disease  when  practised  during  the 
existence  of  an  epidemic.  In  case 
of  vaccination,  he  strongly  advo¬ 
cates  the  strict  enforcement  of  sani¬ 
tation  and  isolation.  He  maintains 
that  personal  and  municipal  cleanli¬ 
ness  is  the  only  scientific  safeguard 
against  zymotic  diseases.  When  the 
authorities  attempted  to  enforce 
vaccination  by  fines  and  imprison¬ 
ment,  Dr.  R.  organized  the  Anti- 
Compulsory  Vaccination  League, 
and  successfully  resisted  what  he 
considered  an  outrage  on  human 
rights.  Dr.  R.  is  a  radical  reformer 
in  religion,  med.,  politics,  sociology 
and  dietetics,  and  a  total  abstainer 
from  intoxicants  and  tobacco.  He 
m.  1857,  Miss  Hester  E.  Harrington. 
Their  only  s. ,  Norman  Garibaldi 
Ross,  a  med.  student  at  Toronto 
Univ.,  has  been  elected  to  the  mem¬ 
bership  of  the  Imp.  Soc.  of  Natur¬ 
alists  of  Moscow,  Russia,  and  of  the 
Imp.  Zool.  Soc.  of  Vienna,  Austria, 
in  recognition  of  his  attainments  in 
entomology.  [D.  at  Detroit,  Mich., 
Oct.  27,  1897.] 

“  He  is  so  thoroughly  sincere,  honest, 
consistent,  conscientious  and  unselfish,  that 
most  men  cannot  understand  him.” — Mail 
and  Empire. 

ROSS,  Rev.  Andrew  W.  (Metli.), 

was  b.  at  Feterangus,  Scot.,  Aug.  13, 
1850,  and  is  the  s.  of  Andrew  Ross, 
by  his  wife,  Ann  Murray  Smith. 
Ed.  at  the  public  sells.,  by  private 
tuition,  and  at  Victoria  Univ.,  he 
was  admitted  as  a  probationer  to 
the  Meth.  ministry,  1872,  and  regu¬ 
larly  ordained,  1877.  In  the  fol¬ 
lowing  year  he  was  apptd.  amission, 
to  the  Indians  on  Lake  Winnipeg, 
and  spent  10  yrs.  at  Beren’s  and 
Fisher  River  reserves,  but  failing 
health  forced  him  to  retire  from  this 
particular  work.  He  was  also  med. 
dispenser  for  the  Indian  Dept., 
1880-88.  He  was  apptd.  Asst.  Secy., 
Man.  and  N.-W.  Conf. ,  1892;  Secy., 
1893;  and  Presdt,  of  Conf.,  1894. 
In  1892  ho  becamo  Presdt.  of  the 
Theol.  Union  of  the  Conf.,  and,  in 
the  same  year,  was  apptd.  Chairman

of  the  Portage  la  Prairie  Dist. , 
which  position,  together  with  the 
pastorate  of  the  ch.  at  that  place,

ROSS,  Arthur  Wellington,  barris¬ 
ter  and  broker,  is  the  eld.  s.  of 
Donald  Ross,  J.P.,  Nairn,  Ont., 
and  was  b.  there,  Mch.  25,  1846. 
Ed.  there,  at  Wardsville  High  Sch., 
at  Toronto  Normal  Sch.  (1st  class 
cert.),  and  at  Toronto  Univ.  (B.A., 
1874),  he  became  Head-master  of 
Cornwall  High  Sch.,  1868,  and 
Inspr.  of  Public  Schs. ,  Glengarry, 
1871.  While  still  a  law  student, 
he  went  to  Man.,  1877,  and  was 
called  to  the  bar  there,  1878. 
Elected  a  Bencher,  1880,  he  prac¬ 
tised  his  profession  in  Winnipeg  for 
some  yrs.  During  the  “  land  fever  ” 
in  Man.  he  invested  largely  in  real 
estate,  devoting  himself  almost  alto¬ 
gether  to  that  business.  He  became 
V.  -P.  of  the  Man.  and  N.  -  W.  Ry.  Co. , 
and  subsequently,  in  1881,  joined 
the  Howland  syndicate  in  its  offer 
to  build  the  Can.  Pac.  Ry.  After¬ 
wards  he  resided  for  6  yrs.  in  B.  C. , 
and,  while  there,  was  instrumental 
in  securing  for  the  city  of  Van¬ 
couver  the  use  of  the  mil.  reserve, 
at  the  entrance  of  the  harbour,  for  a 
park.  He  was  also  one  of  the  first 
to  press  upon  the  attention  of  the 
Ottawa  Govt,  the  desirability  of 
establishing  national  parks  on  the 
line  of  the  C.  P.  Ry.,  and  prepared 
a  report  on  the  subject.  More  re¬ 
cently  he  has  become  interested 
in  the  Rossland  gold  fields,  and  is 
now  head  of  the  firm  of  A.  W. 
Ross  &  Co.,  mining  brokers,  and 
genl.  mangr.  of  the  North  Star  Min¬ 
ing,  Trading  and  Transportation  Co. 
He  sat  for  Springfield,  as  a  Lib.,  in 
the  Man.  Assembly,  1878-82,  and  was 


then  returned  for  Lisgar,  in  the  Ho. 
of  Commons,  as  a  Lib. -Con.  This 
constituency  he  continued  to  repre¬ 
sent  up  to  the  g.  e.  1896,  when  he 
retired  from  political  life.  In  re¬ 
ligion,  a  Presb.,  he  m.  July,  1873, 
Jessie  Flora,  dau.  of  Donald  Cattan- 
ach,  Laggan,  Ont. — 180  Bloor  St. 
E. ,  Toronto;  Rossland,  B.C.;  Mani¬ 
toba  Club  ;  Rideau  Club. 

“  A  man  of  splendid  business  ability.” — 
Can.  American.

Mackenzie  (q.v.),  in  purchasing  the 
Toronto  Ry.  from  the  City  of  To¬ 
ronto,  and  afterwards  rebuilt  its 
tracks,  making  it  an  electric  line. 
In  1892  he  undertook  the  re-organ- 
ization  of  the  Montreal  St.  Ry. , 
changing  it  from  a  horse  line  to  an 
electric  service.  Mr.  R.  has  also 
in  the  same  way  converted  the  st. 
rys.  of  Winnipeg  and  St.  John.  In 
1896  he  and  Mr.  Mackenzie  acquired 
the  tramway  systems  of  Birmingham, 
and  formed  the  City  of  Birmingham 
Tramways  Co.  (Ltd.)  for  the  opera¬ 
tion  of  the  road  under  an  electric 
system,  and,  in  1897,  he,  with  Mr. 
Mackenzie  and  others,  secured  a 
charter  and  franchise  from  the  Govt, 
of  Jamaica  to  build  electric  tram¬ 
ways  on  the  Island.  He  is  V.-P. 
and  Mang.  Dir.  of  the  Montreal  St. 
Ry. ;  V.-P.  of  the  Toronto  Ry.  Co.; 
Presdt.  of  the  Winnipeg  and  St. 
John  St.  Rys.;  Presdt.  of  the  Dom. 
Bridge  Co. ;  Commodore  of  the  Royal 
St.  Lawrence  Yacht  Club  ;  trustee 
of  Bishop’s  Coll.  Univ.,  Lennoxville, 
P.  Q. ;  a  gov.  of  the  Royal  V  ictoria 
Hospital,  and  a  gov.  of  McGill 
Univ.,  Montreal.  He  was  one  of 
the  promoters  of  the  Lake  of  the 
Woods  Milling  Co.,  1887  ;  chief 
promoter  of  the  Columbia  River 
Lumber  Co.,  1889;  and  chief  pro¬ 
moter  of  the  Can.  Land  and  Invest. 
Co.,  1891.  Of  late  yrs.  he  has 
taken  an  active  interest  in  yachting, 
and  was  the  owner  of  the  Glen- 
cairn  which  won  the  Seawanhaka- 
Corinthian  Cup  for  half-raters  in  Am. 
waters,  1896.  He  is  an  adherent  of 
the  Presb.  Ch.,  and  m.  1872,  Miss 
Annie  Kerr. — 360  Peel  St.,  Montreal; 
St.  James's  Club;  Rideau  Club ;  To¬ 
ronto  Club ;  Manitoba  Club  ;  Players' 
Club,  New  York. 

ROSS,  Rev.  James  (Presb.),  edu¬ 
cationist,  is  the  s.  of  Jas.  Ross,  who 
came  to  Can.  with  the  rest  of  his 
family,  1853.  B.  in  Peterculter, 
Aberdeenshire,  Scot.,  Aug.  19,  1851, 
he  attended  the  schs.  in  his  native 
place,  and  after  coming  to  Can., 
1869,  taught  sell,  for  some  yrs. 
Entering  Queen’s  Univ.,  Kingston, 
he  graduated  B.A.,  187S,  and  M.  A. 


and  B.D. ,  1881,  holding  a  scholar¬ 
ship  every  ear  during  his  entire 
course.  He  was  ordained  and  in¬ 
ducted  pastor  of  Knox  Ch. ,  Perth, 
Ont.,  1881  ;  declined  a  call  to  St. 
Andrew’s  Ch.,  Ottawa,  1883;  was 
Lecturer  in  Ch.  History  in  Queen’s 
Univ.,  1890-92;  and  wasapptd.  Prof, 
of  Practical  Theol.  in  the  Presb. 
Coll. ,  Montreal,  1892.  Hem.  Oct., 
1883,  Agnes,  dau.  of  Danl.  Mc- 
Naughton,  Camilla,  Ont.— 22  Sum- 
merhill  A  ve.,  Montreal. 

“A  man  of  Christian  character  and  spirit, 
with  ability  and  scholarly  attainments.” — 
Rev.  Principal  Mac  Vicar. 

ROSS,  Hon.  James  Hamilton,  legis¬ 
lator,  is  the  s.  of  John  Edgar  Ross, 
formerly  of  London,  Ont.,  and  now 
of  Moose  J aw,  N.  W.  T.  B.  in  Lon¬ 
don,  May  12,  1856,  he  was  ed.  at 
the  Grammar  Sch.  there,  and  pro¬ 
ceeded  to  the  Territories,  1882,  where 
he  became  a  rancher.  In  Aug.,  1883, 
he  was  elected  to  the  N.  -  W.  Council, 
and,  in  1888,  to  the  Assembly,  of 
which  he  became  Speaker,  1891.  In 
1 896  he  was  apptd.  to  the  Ex.  Comte, 
for  the  Territories,  and,  in  Oct. ,  1897, 
assumed  office  as  Comnr.  of  Public 
Works  and  Secy,  in  Mr.  Haultain’s 
Cabinet.  He  was  an  unsuccessful 
candidate  for  Western  Assiniboia 
at  the  Dom.  g.  e.  1887  (Vote:  N.  E. 
Davin,  C. ,  726  ;  J.  H.  Ross,  L. , 
423).  Politically,  he  is  a  Lib.  He 
m.  Dec.,  1886,  Miss  Barbara  E. 
McKay.  —  Regina  ;  Moose  Jaw, 
N.  W.  T. 

ROSS,  Rev.  James  Stewart  (Meth.), 
is  the  s.  of  Jas.  Ross,  by  his  wife, 
Jane  Stewart,  both  natives  of  Dun¬ 
dee,  Scot.,  and  now  living  at  Fergus, 
Ont.  B.  at  Kingston,  Ont.,  1848, 
he  was  ed.  at  the  public  sch.,  Fer¬ 
gus  ;  at  the  High  Sch.,  Cobourg  ; 
and  at  Victoria  Univ.,  Cobourg 
(B.A.,  1875;  M.A.,  1880;  D.D., 
1894).  He  obtained  a  1st  class  cert, 
and  was  a  public  sch.  teacher,  1864- 
67,  when  he  joined  the  ministry  of 
the  Meth.  Ch.  He  became  Secy,  of 
the  Niagara  Annual  Conf. ,  1867  ; 
Asst.  Secy.  Genl.  Conf.,  Montreal, 
1890  ;  Chairman  of  Dist.,  1891  ;  and 
Presdt.  of  Niagara  Annual  Conf.,

1893.  He  is  a  mem.  of  the  Bd.  of 
Regents  and  a  Senator  of  Victoria 
Univ.;  a  mem.  of  the  Bd.  of  Govs., 
and  a  Senator  of  the  Wesl.  Theol. 
Coll.,  Montreal;  V.-P.  of  the  Ont. 
Lord’s  Day  Alliance ;  and  Presdt. 
of  the  Oxford  Co.  Prohibitory  Assn. 
He  is  the  author  of  “  Trials  and 
Triumphs  of  Prohibition  ”  ;  “  An 
Appeal  for  the  Immediate  Suppres¬ 
sion  of  the  Liquor  Traffic”  ;  “The 
First  Hundred  Yrs.  of  Modern  Mis¬ 
sions  ”  ;  and  of  various  articles  in  the 
Can.  Meth.  Mag.  He  believes  that 
no  other  political  issue  is  half  so

welfare  of  this  nation  as  the  total 
suppression  by  law  of  the  liquor

“As  a  public  speaker,  theologian  and

ROSS,  Hon.  John  Jones,  Senator,  is 
the  s.  of  the  late  G.  McIntosh  Ross, 
formerly  a  W est  Indian  merchant, 
by  his  wife,  Marie  Louise  Gouin. 
B.  in  Quebec,  Aug.  16,  1832,  he  was 
ed.  at  the  Quebec  Semy. ,  and  was 
admitted  to  the  med.  profession, 
1853.  He  entered  public  life  as 
mem.  for  Champlain  in  the  old  Can. 
Assembly,  g.  e.  1861.  At  the  Union, 
1867,  he  was  returned  for  the  same 
constituency  to  both  the  Ho.  of 
Commons  and  the  Quebec  Assembly, 
but  was  apptd.  soon  afterwards  to 
the  Leg.  Council.  He  continued  to 
represent  Champlain  in  the  Com¬ 
mons  up  to  the  g.  e.  1874,  when  he 
retired  from  that  Chamber.  He  was 
called  to  the  Senate,  Apl.  12,  1887, 
and  continues  therein.  Dr.  R.  has 
always  been  a  Con.,  and  was  a  con¬ 
sistent  supporter  of  Sir  John  Mac¬ 
donald  and  Sir  Geo.  Cartier,  in  re¬ 
ference  to  the  Confederation  of  the 
Provinces,  the  acquisition  of  the 
N.W.T.,  the  construction  of  the 
Can.  Pacific  Ry.  and  the  “  N.  P.” 
Entering  the  Quebec  Govt.,  Feb., 
1873,  he  was  for  many  yrs.  a  mem. 


of  successive  Provl.  Cabinets,  and, 
from  Jan.,  1884  to  Jan.,  1887  held 
the  Premiership  of  Quebec.  He 
became  Speaker  of  the  Senate,  Sept. 
14,  1891,  remaining  as  such  up  to 
the  close  of  the  7th  Parlt.,  1896. 
On  May  1,  1896,  he  entered  the 
Tupper  Admn. ,  without  portfolio, 
and  retired  with  his  colleagues  in 
July,  same  year,  after  the  defeat  of 
the  Govt.  Dr.  R.  was  elected 
Presdt.  of  the  Coll,  of  Phys.  and 
Surgs.,  Quebec,  1889.  He  has  been 
also  a  mem.  of  the  Agricul.  Council 
of  Quebec,  and  V.-P.  of  the  North 
Shore  Ry.  In  religious  faith,  he  is 
a  R.  C.  He  m.  1856,  Arline,  dau. 
of  Lt.-Col.  Lanouette,  Champlain. — 
Ste.  Anne  de  la  Perade,  P.Q. 

“A  man  of  scrupulous  honesty  and  up¬ 
right  character,  who  has  conscientiously 
administered  the  affairs  of  the  Province.” — 
Gazette. 

ROSS,  Philip  Dansken,  journalist, 
is  the  s.  of  P.  S.  Ross  (q.v.),  and 
was  b.  in  Montreal,  Jan.  1,  1858. 
Ed.  at  private  schs. ,  he  graduated 
B.Ap.Sc.,  at  McGill  Univ.,  1878. 
Dropping  engineering  as  a  profession, 
he  joined  the  staff  of  the  Montreal 
Star,  as  a  reporter,  1879 ;  and  that  of 
the  Toronto  Mail,  1880.  He  became 
asst.  ed.  Toronto  Mews,  1882  ;  mang. 
ed.  Montreal  Star,  1885;  ed.  and  part 
prop,  of  the  Ottawa  Journal,  Jan., 
1887  ;  and  sole  prop,  of  do.,  Nov., 
1891.  He  has  filled  the  vice-presi¬ 
dency  of  the  Can.  Press  Assn.,  and 
has  been  for  some  yrs.  a  mem.  of  the 
Council  of  the  Ottawa  Bd.  of  Trade. 
Mr.  R.  has  always  taken  an  active 
interest  in  athletics,  and  was  a  popu¬ 
lar  figure  at  one  time  among  the 
athletes  of  Montreal  and  Toronto. 
He  was  elected  Presdt.  A.  A.  Assn, 
of  Can.,  1891  ;  Presdt.  Ottawa 
Hockey  Club,  1895  ;  and  Presdt. 
O.  A.  A.  C.  Bicycle  Club,  same  year. 
Politically  Ind.,  he  is  a  Free  Trader 
in  principle,  but  believes  local  cir¬ 
cumstances  may  justify  protective 
duties  at  times.— Elgin  St.,  Ot¬ 
tawa  ;  Rideau  Club. 

“Mr.  Ross  was  foremost  among  the  Ot¬ 
tawa  Equal  Righters  in  the  protest  against 
the  Jesuit  bill,  having  clone  good  service  in 
the  struggle.  His  newspaper  has  been  in¬ 
dependent,  patriotic,  fearlessly  outspoken.

ROSS,  Philip  S.,  chartered  ac¬ 
countant,  was  b.  of  Scottish  parent¬ 
age,  at  Belfast,  Irel. ,  Aug.,  1827. 
Ed.  at  Glasgow,  Scot.,  he  received 
his  business  training  in  the  service 
of  the  Monkland  Iron  and  Steel  Co. , 
Soot.,  and  came  to  Montreal,  June, 
1851.  Following  a  mercantile  career 
there  for  some  yrs.,  he  retired  there¬ 
from  on  his  appt.  as  Official  Assignee 
under  the  Insolvent  Act,  1874.  On 
the  organization  of  the  Chartered 
Accountants  into  a  separate  body, 
he  was  chosen  Y.  -P. ,  and  since  then 
has  been  elected  Presdt.  of  the  Assn. 
He  is  an  active  mem.  of  the  Montreal 
Bd.  of  Trade,  and  he  holds  comns. 
from  nearly  all  the  Provl.  Govts., 
empowering  him  to  take  affidavits 
for  use  in  their  respective  provinces. 
Among  other  offices  held  by  him, 
he  is  Secy,  of  the  Sailors’  Institute.

ROUTH,  Edward  John,  education¬ 
ist,  is  the  s.  of  the  late  Com  my. - 
Genl.  Sir  R.  J.  Routh,  K.C.B.,  by 
his  wife,  Marie  Louise,  sister  of  H.  E. 
Cardinal  Taschereau.  B.  in  Quebec, 
1831,  he  accompanied  his  parents 
to  Eng. ,  at  the  age  of  1 1 ,  and  sub¬ 
sequently  was  sent  to  Univ.  Coll. 
Sell.,  where  he  stayed  only  a  year 
before  entering  Univ.  Coll.  Here  he 
made  rapid  progress  in  math,  studies, 
under  Prof.  De  Morgan.  He  passed 
through  the  higher  classes,  gaining 
the  math,  prizes  at  the  yearly  exams. 
This  encouraged  him  to  attend  the 
matriculation  exam,  in  the  Univ.  of 
London,  1847,  and  afterwards  the 
B.  A.  exam.,  1849,  gaining  the  math, 
scholarship  at  each.  He  received 
also  the  gold  medal  at  his  M.  A. 
exam.,  1853.  In  Oct.,  1851,  he 
entered  Peterhouse,  Cambridge.  He 
studied  for  a  year  under  Mr.  Tod- 


I  hunter,  of  St.  John’s  Coll.,  and  for

under  Mr.  Hopkins,  of  Peterhouse. 
In  1854  he  graduated  as  Senior 
Wrangler,  and  at  the  Smith’s  prize 
exam,  he  was  bracketed  equal  with 
Mr.  Maxwell,  afterwards  Prof,  of 
Experimental  Phil,  at  Cambridge. 
He  was  then  elected  a  Fellow  of 
Peterhouse,  and  adopted  the  profes¬ 
sion  of  teaching  as  his  career  in  life. 
From  1861  to  1885  (with  one  excep¬ 
tion,  1883)  the  Senior  Wrangler  was 
every  year  his  pupil,  besides  twice 
before  that  date  ;  in  all  26  times. 
He  has  also  had  amongst  his  pupils 
41  Smith’s  prizemen.  This  success 
is  without  precedent.  In  1855  Mr. 
R.  wrote  a  book  in  conjunction  with 
Lord  Brougham.  In  1859  he  was 
apptd.  examr.  in  Math,  in  the  Univ. 
of  London,  and,  after  the  necessary 
interval  of  a  year,  he  held  the  office 
for  a  second  quinquennial  period 
( 1865-70).  Soon  after  his  graduation 
he  was  elected  a  mem.  of  the  Cam¬ 
bridge  Phil.  Soc.,  of  the  Geol.  Soc., 
and  of  the  Royal  Geog.  Soc.  ;  subse¬ 
quently,  he  became  a  mem.  of  the 
Astronom.  Soc.  and  a  Fellow  of  the 
Royal  Soc.  He  is  also  an  original 
mem.  of  the  London  Math.  Soc., 
having  been  one  of  those  who  helped 
to  establish  it.  In  1860  he  was 
moderator,  and,  in  1861,  examr.  for 
the  Math.  Tripos  at  Cambridge.  In 
1864  he  m.  the  eld.  dau.  of  Sir  G.  B. 
Airy,  K.C.B.,  the  late  Astronomer- 
Royal.  In  1 867  he  gained  the  Adams 
prize  for  his  essay  on  the  “Stability  of 
Motion.”  The  hon.  degree  of  LL.  D. 
was  conferred  upon  him  in  1879  by 
the  Univ.  of  Glasgow.  In  1883  he 
was  one  of  the  first  to  take  the  degree 
of  Doctor  of  Science,  then  estab¬ 
lished  in  the  Univ.  of  Cambridge  for 
those  who  have  “  given  proof  of  dis¬ 
tinction  by  some  original  contribu¬ 
tion  to  the  advancement  of  science.” 
He  was  elected  hon.  Fellow  of  Peter¬ 
house  the  same  year.  In  1884  Dr. 
R.  was  apptd.  by  the  Crown  a  Fel¬ 
low  of  the  Univ.  of  London,  and  has

!  body  of  that  univ.  He  has  written

ROUTHIER,  Hon.  Adolphe  Basile, 

judge  and  jurist,  is  the  s.  of  Chas. 
Routhier,  a  farmer,  whose  ancestors 
came  to  Can.  from  Saintonge,  France. 
B.  at  St.  Placide,  P.Q.,  May  8,  1839, 
he  was  ed.  at  the  Coll.,  Ste.  Th6r6se, 
and  at  Laval  Univ.  (B.A.,  1858). 
He  also  graduated  B.  C.  L.  at  the  last- 
named  institution,  and  was  called 
to  the  bar,  1861,  commencing  the 
practice  of  his  profession  at  Kam- 
ouraska.  A  Con.  in  politics,  he 
was  on  two  occasions,  in  1869  and  in 
1872,  an  unsuccessful  candidate  in 
that  party’s  interests  for  the  repre¬ 
sentation  of  the  Co.  of  Kamouraska 
in  the  Ho.  of  Commons.  Created  a 
Q.  C.,  by  the  Earl  of  Dufferin,  1S73, 
he  was,  in  Sept,  of  the  same  year, 
raised  to  the  bench,  as  a  Puisne  J udge 
of  the  Sup.  Ct. ,  P.  Q.  His  Lordship 
was  at  first  assigned  to  the  Saguenay 
Dist.,  but  in  Dec.,  1889,  he  was 
transferred  to  the  Dist.  of  Quebec, 
where  he  still  resides.  He  is  re¬ 
garded  as  “  a  painstaking  judge, 
having  a  profound  knowledge  of 
law,  and  whose  decisions  are  marked 
by  great  clearness  and  soundness.” 


Before  his  call  to  the  bench,  Mr.  R. 
had  disclosed  marked  talents  as  a 
public  writer.  Had  he  remained  in 
journalism  he  would  undoubtedly 
have  won  renown  as  one  of  the  most 
brilliant  and  aggressive  political 
writers  of  his  time.  It  was  at  this 
period  that  he  published  his  “  Cau- 
series  du  dimanche,”  and  his  “Por¬ 
traits  et  Pastels  Littbraires,”  the 
latter  under  the  nom  de  plume  of 
“Jean  Piquefort.”  He  is  not  less 
noted  for  his  powers  of  oratory.  In 
1875  he  made  a  tour  of  the  Brit. 
Isles  and  of  Belgium,  France  and 
Italy,  and  while  at  Rome  was  apptd, 
by  the  Pope,  a  Knight  Commander 
of  the  Order  of  St.  Gregory.  On 
his  return  to  Can.  he  delivered  a 
course  of  lectures  at  Laval  Univ. 
(in  which  institution  he  is  Prof,  of 
Internl.  Law),  which  added  greatly 
to  his  reputation  as  an  observer,  a 
thinker  and  a  speaker.  His  later 
discourses  in  connection  with  the 
celebration  of  St.  Jean  Baptiste, 
the  visit  of  Albani  and  the  Centen¬ 
ary  of  Christopher  Columbus,  have 
all  been  notable  utterances.  His 
Lordship  received  the  hon.  degree 
of  Lit.D.,  from  Laval  Univ.,  1880; 
and  that  of  LL.  D. ,  from  the  same 
seat  of  learning,  1883.  He  is  also  a 
Fellow  of  the  Royal  Soc.  of  Can. 
His  magnum  opus,  as  a  literary 
man,  is  undoubtedly  “A  Travers 
l’Europe”  (2vols.,  1882-83).  Among 
his  other  works  are:  “  En  Canot” 
(1881) ;  “Les  Echos’’  (pofemes,  1883); 
“A  Travers  l’Espagne”  (1889); 
“Les  Grands  Drames”  (1890);  “Con¬ 
ferences  et  Discourses”  (do.);  “  De 
Quebec  k  Victoria”  (1863).  In 
1893  he  wrote  the  introduction  to  a 
new  edition  of  the  Repertoire  Na¬ 
tional,  which  served  at  once  as 
an  introduction  and  a  commentary. 
He  was  apptd.  Judge  of  the  Ct.  of 
Vice-Admiralty,  Quebec,  vice  Irvine, 
May,  1897,  and  was  elected,  the 
same  year,  Genl.  Presdt.  of  the  St. 
Jean  Bapt.  Soc.  In  1897  he  declined 
appt.  to  the  Lt. -Governorship  of  the 
N..W.  T.  A  mem.  of  the  R.  C.  Ch., 
he  m.  1862,  Marie  Clorinde,  only 
dau.  of  the  late  J.  0.  Mondelet,

bourg  Grammar  Sch. ,  which,  under

ROYAL,  Hon.  Joseph,  advocate, 
journalist  and  legislator,  was  b.  at 
Repentigny,  P.Q.,  May  7,  1837.  Ed. 
at  that  place,  he  completed  his 
studies  at  St.  Mary’s  (Jesuit)  Coll., 
Montreal.  He  commenced  his  jour¬ 
nalistic  career  on  La  Minerve, 
Montreal,  1857  ;  established  L’Ordre, 
1859 ;  and  founded  Le  Nouveau 
Monde,  1857.  He  likewise  assisted 
in  founding,  1864,  La  Revue  Can., 
one  of  the  ablest  conducted  periodi¬ 
cals  ever  established  in  Can.,  and 
contributed  to  it  many  interesting 
political  papers,  including  his  “Vie 
Politique  de  Sir  Louis  H.  Lafon- 
taine.”  Called  to  the  bar,  1864,  he 
did  not  for  the  moment  follow  the 
active  practice  of  the  legal  profes¬ 
sion,  his  whole  time  being  devoted 
to  literary  and  newspaper  work. 
He  took  an  active  part  in  organizing 
the  Papal  Zouave  brigade,  sent  from 
Quebec  to  the  assistance  of  the 
Holy  Father,  1867-68.  Removing 
to  Man.,  1870,  he  established,  at 
Winnipeg,  the  paper  Le  Metis, 
which,  in  1882,  became  Le  Manitoba. 
From  this  time  until  1880  he  was 
in  active  pi’actice  at  the  local  bar, 
and  was  retained  in  many  notable 
cases,  including  the  defence  of  the 
prisoners  Lepine  aud  Naud,  who 
were  tried  at  the  Man.  Criminal 
Assizes,  Oct.,  1874,  for  the  murder 
of  Thos.  Scott  by  the  Provisional 
Govt,  of  Louis  Riel.  Elected  to  the 
first  Legislature  given  to  Man.,  1870, 
he  remained  a  mem.  of  that  body

RUTHERFORD,  John,  M.E.,  is  the 

s.  of  Robt.  Rutherford,  by  Mary,  his 
wife.  B.  at  Swallwell,  Durham,  Eng., 
June,  1823,  he  was  ed.  at  a  private 
sch.,  and  at  16  was  placed  with  a 
civil  engr.  of  considerable  repute,  and 
passed  thence  to  the  engine  building 
shops  of  Thos.  Richardson  &  Sons, 
where  he  gained  a  practical  know¬ 
ledge  of  machinery.  A  dullness  in 
trade  and  other  circumstances  lead¬ 
ing  to  the  abandonment  of  civil 
engineering  as  a  profession,  he  was 
next  articled  to  Mr.  (now  Sir  Geo. ) 
Elliott,  the  eminent  mining  engr. 
and  coal  owner,  and  was  his  first 
pupil.  On  leaving  him  he  was  for 
a  time  at  the  Seaham  and  Seaton 
collieries,  then  being  opened  by  the 
Marquis  of  Londonderry,  and  was 
shortly  afterwards  apptd.  a  mining 
asst,  in  Lord  Durham’s  extensive 
collieries.  In  1865,  a  delegation  from 
N.  S.  having  arrived  in  Eng.  to  secure 
the  services  of  a  competent  person 
for  the  office  of  Inspr.  of  Mines  for 
that  province,  Mr.  R.  was  selected 
for  it.  After  6  yrs.  he  resigned,  and 
became  Genl.  Mangr.  of  the  Genl. 
Mining  Assn,  of  London,  the  oldest, 
and  at  one  time  the  only,  coal  co.  in 
N.  S.  This  position,  after  5  yrs.,  he 
also  resigned.  Entering  into  private 
practice  as  a  mining  engr.,  he  was 
consulted  and  employed  as  such  in 
many  places,  including  N.  B.,  Utah 
and  Spain.  After  the  explosion  at 
the  Albion  Mines,  N.S.,  in  1880,  he 
was  sent  out  to  assist  in  replacing 
the  mines  in  a  productive  condition. 
Subsequently,  he  was  apptd.  mangr. 
there,  and  remained  until  the  Vale 
and  Halifax  cos.  were  amalgamated 
with  the  Acadia  Coal  Co.  He  has 
been  a  mem.  of  the  North  of  Eng. 
Inst,  of  Mining  Engrs.  since  its  for¬ 
mation,  1852,  and  has  contributed  to 
its  “Trans.,”  as  well  as  to  various 
other  publications,  articles  on  the 
coals  and  minerals  of  N.  S.  He  was 
for  some  yrs.  Examr.  in  Mining  at 
King’s  Coll.,  N.S.,  and  on  the  estab¬ 
lishment  by  the  N.  S.  Govt,  of  a  Bd. 
of  Examrs.  for  granting  certs,  to 
candidates  for  the  grades  of  mine 
officials,  he  was  elected  Chairman  of

RYAN,  Rev.  Francis  (R.  C.),  was 
b.  in  Newfoundland,  of  Irish  parent¬ 
age,  1844.  Ed.  there  and  inlrel. , 
France  and  Eng.,  he  graduated  in 
Phil,  and  Theol.  with  the  Jesuits, 
and  was  ordained  priest,  Sept.  19, 
1875.  Soon  afterwards  he  came  to 
Can.,  as  his  Secy.,  with  the  late 
Papal  Del.  Apostolic,  the  Most  Rev. 
Geo.  Conroy,  whose  pupil  he  had 
been  in  Irel.,  and  with  whom  he 
was  a  great  favourite.  After  the 
death  of  his  distinguished  and  dearly 
loved  friend,  Father  R.  came  to 
Montreal,  and  was  Eng.  preacher  in 
the  J esuits’  Ch. ,  in  that  city,  for  2 
yrs.  From  Montreal  he  went  to  the 
U  S.,  and  taught  Phil,  at  St.  John’s 
Coll.,  Fordham,  and  at  St.  Francis 
Xavier’s  Coll.,  N.  Y.  City.  He  was 
afterwards  pastor  of  St.  Ignatius 
Ch.,  Baltimore,  and  of  the  Ch.  of 
the  Holy  Trinity,  Chicago.  He  gave 
ecclesiastical  retreats  to  the  clergy 
of  the  leading  dioceses  in  the  U.  S. 
and  Can.,  and  was  and  is  favourably 
known  as  a  successful  public  lecturer 
and  an  eloquent  and  impressive 
pulpit  orator.  For  some  yrs.  he  has 
been  Rector  of  St.  Michael’s  Cath. , 
Toronto.  He  was  elected  a  mem.  of 
the  Genl.  Ex.  Comte,  of  the  Pan- Am. 
Congress,  May,  1895,  and  a  mem.  of 
the  Toronto  Univ.  Senate,  1896.  In 
the  same  year  he  was  apptd.  a  del. 
to  the  Irish  National  Convention, 
Dublin,  Irel.  He  has  lectured  on 
art  and  other  subjects  before  the 
Women’s  Art.  Assn.,  Toronto.  — 
A  rchbishop’ s  Palace,  Toronto. 


RYAN,  Hugh,  contractor  and 
capitalist,  was  b.  in  Limerick,  Irel., 
July,  1832.  Coming  to  Can.  with 
his  parents,  1841,  he  lived  with 
them  near  the  city  of  Montreal, 
until  1850.  In  that  year  he  com¬ 
menced  his  business  career,  being 
employed  on  the  St.  Lawrence  and 
Atlantic  Ry.  (now  forming  a  portion 
of  the  Grand  Trunk  system)  then 
being  built  under  Sir  C.  S.  Gzowski. 
Not  long  afterwards,  he  undertook, 
in  partnership  with  his  bro. ,  a  con¬ 
tract  for  the  construction  of  a  por¬ 
tion  of  the  Brockville  and  Ottawa 
Ry.,  running  from  Smith’s  Falls  to 
Perth,  and  also  for  the  sec.  of  the 
same  road  between  Arnprior  and 
Bonnecliere.  Contracts  in  Michi¬ 
gan,  Ill.,  Kentucky,  N.  S.,  Maine, 
and  N.  B.  followed,  Mr.  R.  being 
associated  in  some  of  his  works 
with  the  late  A.  Brooks,  of  Brock¬ 
ville,  and  with  the  late  P.  Purcell, 
of  Cornwall.  Among  his  most  im¬ 
portant  and  successful  undertakings 
were  twenty  miles  of  the  Intercl. 
Ry. ,  including  the  heavy  work  con¬ 
nected  with  the  bridges  over  the 
Miramichi  River ;  the  sec.  of  the 
C.  P.  Ry.  from  Fort  William  west 
to  the  Eagle  River,  over  230  miles  ; 
the  Red  River  Valley  Ry. ,  from 
Winnipeg ;  and  the  Sault  Ste.  Marie 
Canal,  the  latter  of  which  before 
completion  occupied  6  yrs.  of  his 
active  and  useful  life.  Mr.  R. 
also  undertook  the  management  dur¬ 
ing  construction  of  the  C.  P.  Ry. 
line  from  Toronto  to  Perth.  He 
was  one  of  the  promoters  of  the 
Dom.  Cable  Co.,  1882,  and  was 
elected  an  assoc,  of  the  Can.  Soc.  of 
C.  E.,  1888.  Some  yrs.  ago  he  re¬ 
moved  his  residence  from  Perth  to 
Toronto.  In  Nov.,  1895,  he  gave 
evidence  of  his  philanthropic  spirit 
by  erecting  and  fitting  up  a  wing  to 
St.  Michael’s  Hospital,  in  the  latter 
city,  for  the  use  and  benefit  of 
patients  of  all  denominations,  at 
a  cost  of  .$40,000.  Mr.  R.  is  a 
Govt,  trustee  of  the  Toronto  Genl. 
Hospital.  He  is  also  a  dir.  of  the 
!  Freehold  Loan  and  Savings  Co.,  of 
I  the  Can.  Genl.  Electric  Co.,  of  the

RYAN,  Peter,  Ont.  public  service, 
is  the  s.  of  Bernard  Ryan,  a  native 
of  Ryan’s  Town,  Co.  Down,  Irel.,  by 
his  wife,  Susannah  Tait,  and  was  b. 
at  Carlisle,  Eng.,  Aug.  23,  1842.  Ed. 
at  the  Ch.  Sch.,  Carlisle,  and  else¬ 
where,  he  became  a  horse  and  cattle 
trader,  and  was,  subsequently,  an 
auctioneer  and  hardware  dealer. 
Coming  to  Can.,  he  entered  the, ser¬ 
vice  of  the  Joseph  Hall  Agricul. 
Works,  Oshawa.  He  sat  as  an  aid. 
in  the  Toronto  City  Council,' 1879-83, 
and,  in  1880,  unsuccessfully  opposed 
Dr.  J as.  Beatty  in  West  Toronto  for 
the  Ho.  of  Commons.  In  religion,  a 
R.  C. ;  politically,  he  is  a  Reformer. 
He  is  also  a  life-long  abstainer.  He 
believes  in  the  abolition  of  war,  and 
favours  an  Ind.  Republic  in  Can. 
Mr.  R.  has  been  for  many  yrs.  an 
active  political  organizer  and  speaker 
on  the  Lib.  side  in  Ont.,  and  in  re¬ 
ward  for  his  party  services  was 
apptd.  Regr.  of  Deeds,  East  Toronto, 
Jan.  1,  1890.  This  office  he  still  re¬ 
tains.  He  m.  July,  1861,  Miss  Margt. 
McConnell. — 51  Grosvenor  St.,  To¬ 
ronto,  Ont.

SADLIER,  Mrs.  Mary  Anne,  au¬ 
thor,  is  the  eld.  dau.  of  Francis 
Madden,  of  Cootehill,  Co.  Cavan, 
Irel.  B.  there,  Dec.  21,  1820,  she 
was  ed.  partly  by  private  tuition 
and  partly  at  a  private  sch.  When 
scarcely  18,  she  began  to  contribute 
to  La  Belle  Assemblee  (Lond. ),  a 
mag.  published  under  the  patronage 
of  the  late  Duchess  of  Kent.  After 
coming  to  Can.  she  m.  Nov.,  1846, 
Jas.  Sadlier,  a  younger  mem.  of  the 
firm  of  D.  &  J.  Sadlier,  publishers, 
N.  Y.,  Boston  and  Montreal  (he  d. 
1869).  One  of  her  first  works  was 
a  collection  of  traditionary  stories, 
published  in  Montreal,  entitled 
‘  ‘  Tales  of  the  Olden  Time.  ”  In  one 
of  her  numerous  tales  of  Irish  immi¬ 
grant  life  and  adventure,  called 
“  Eleanor  Preston,”  there  are  some 
sketches  of  Lower  Can.  rural  life  and 
scenery,  which  go  to  show  that  the 
faculty  of  close  observation  had 
developed  itself  very  early  in  her 
case.  Mrs.  S.’s  literary  works  may 
be  divided  into  three  classes  :  (1) 
The  historical  Irish  romance,  of 
which  the  “  Confederate  Chieftains” 
is  the  best  and  most  elaborate  ;  (2) 
her  didactic  and  religious  works, 
original  and  translated,  of  which 
1  ‘  De  Ligny’s  Life  of  the  Blessed 
Virgin  ”  may  be  cited  as  an  example ; 
and  (3)  a  dept,  or  sub-dept.  of 
fiction,  in  which  Thos.  D’Arcy  Mc¬ 
Gee  considered  her  wholly  un¬ 
rivalled,  and  which  may  be  called 
the  romance  of  Irish  immigration. 
Under  this  last  head  may  be  in¬ 
cluded  her  “Willy  Burke,”  “The 
Blakes  and  Flanagans,”  “  Con 
O’Regan,”  “  Eleanor  Preston,” 
“Aunt  Honor’s  Keepsake,”  etc. 
In  all,  Mrs.  S.  is  the  author  of  some 
60  works,  original  and  translated. 
One  of  the  latest  of  her  productions 
is  “  The  Poems  of  Thos.  D’Arcy 
McGee,  with  an  introduction  and 
biographical  sketch”  (1886).  Mrs. 
S.  was  the  ed.  for  some  yrs.  of  the 
N.  Y.  Tablet  newspaper,  and  had

and  provision  business.  On  his 
father’s  death,  he  succeeded  him  as 
head  of  the  firm,  which  then  be¬ 
came  F.  X.  St.  Charles  &  Co.  He 
is  a  J.  P.,  and  sat  for  some  yrs.  in 
the  City  Council.  He  was  also  on 
the  Comte,  of  Management  of  the 
Corn  Exchange.  He  was  one  of  the 
founders  of  La  Banque  d’Hochelaga, 
1874,  and  became  its  first  Presdt.,  a 
position  he  has  retained  up  to  the 
present  time.  He  is  one  of  the 
governors  and  Treas.  of  Laval 
Univ.,  Montreal.  In  religion,  a 
R.  C.,  hem.  Miss  Marie  Delphine 
Tessier.  Politically,  he  is  a  mod. 
Con.  His  nephew,  J.  St.  Charles, 
has  achieved  distinction  as  an  artist

the  gold  medal,  and  declared  ‘  ‘  hors 
concours”  by  the  Prole  des  Beaux

the  Salon. — 336  St.  Denis  St.,  Mont¬

ST.  PIERRE,  Henri  Cesaire,  Q.C., 
is  the  s.  of  the  late  Joseph  St. 
Pierre,  a  patriot  of  ’37,  by  his  wife, 
Domitilde  Denis.  B.  at  Ste.  Made¬ 
leine,  P.Q.,  Sept.  13,  1S44,  he  was 
ed.  at  the  Montreal  Coll.,  and,  sub¬ 
sequently,  studied  law  with  City 
Atty.  Agnew,  of  Kingston,  Ont. 
The  Am.  civil  war  was  then  at  its 
height,  and  young  St,  P.,  yielding 
to  a  desire  for  a  mil.  life,  joined  the 
Northern  forces.  He  served  in  the 
76th  N.  Y.  Volunteers,  but  being 
wounded  in  Va.,  in  the  autumn  of 
1863,  was  captured  by  the  enemy, 
and  remained  a  prisoner  of  war  in 
the  South  until  the  close  of  the  war. 
Resuming  his  law  studies  in  the 
office  of  the  late  Sir  Geo.  Cartier, 
Montreal,  he  was  called  to  the 
bar,  1870,  has  since  practised  his 
profession  in  Montreal,  and  is  now 
regarded  as  “probably  the  leading 
criminal  lawyer  of  the  Province  ” 
(Toronto  Mail).  It  has  been  stated 
that  he  has  defended  more  than  30 
persons  accused  of  capital  offences,

dians.”  In  religion,  a  R.  C.,  he  m. 
1874,  Adeline  Albina,  dau.  of  the 
late  Adolphe  Lesieur,  merchant, 
Terrebonne. — iJJ  Berri  St.,  Mont¬

SANDHAM,  Henry,  R.C.A.,  bro. 
of  the  preceding,  was  b.  in  Mont¬ 
real,  May  24,  1842,  and  was  eel. 
there.  After  spending  some  mths. 
in  the  country  with  his  father,  he 
returned  to  Montreal  and  entered 
the  employ  of  the  late  W.  Notman, 
photographer  to  the  Queen,  whose 
partner  he  subsequently  became. 
From  his  earliest  yrs.  young  S.  was 
fond  of  drawing,  but  he  had  never 
received  any  artistic  tuition.  By 
Mr.  Notman  he  was  placed  under 
the  charge  of  J.  A.  Fraser  (q.v.), 
then  at  the  head  of  the  Art  Dept, 
of  Notman’s  establishment,  and  who 
has  since  so  highly  distinguished 
himself  as  a  painter.  He  had  also 
the  advantage  of  personal  instruc¬ 
tion  from  Vogt,  Way  and  Jacobi.  ' 
Mr.  S.  at  once  took  a  leading  place 
in  all  branches  of  his  profession. 


Later,  he  proceeded  to  Europe  for 
further  study,  and  on  his  return, 
1880,  took  up  his  residence  in  Bos¬ 
ton.  Here  he  is  much  in  request, 
both  as  a  portrait  painter  and  as  a 
painter  of  bat  tle  scenes  and  historical 
occurrences.  He  excels  as  an  illus¬ 
trator  of  books  and  mags. ,  examples 
of  his  work  being  frequently  seen  in 
the  high-class  publications  of  Lon¬ 
don,  Boston  and  N.  Y.  Of  portraits, 
one  of  his  best  is  that  of  the  late  Sir 
John  Macdonald,  Prime  Minister  of 
Can.,  which  was  executed  for  the 
Dom.  Govt.,  Ottawa.  Of  historic 
paintings,  his  “Battle  of  Lexing¬ 
ton,”  executed  for  the  town  of 
Lexington  at  a  cost  of  S4,000,  his 
“  March  of  Time,”  and  his  “  Found¬ 
ing  of  Maryland,”  are  probably  the 
best  known.  On  the  formation  of 
the  Royal  Can.  Acad,  of  Art,  1880,  he 
was  chosen  to  be  an  Academician  by 
the  founders,  the  Marquis  of  Lome 
and  the  Princess  Louise.  Mr.  S. 
m.  1872,  Agnes,  eld.  dau.  of  the  late 
John  Fraser  (“Cousin  Sandy”), 
Montreal,  a  lady  who  has  herself 
acquired  a  high  reputation  among 
artistes. — 164  Boyleston  St.,  Boston, 
Mass.

SANFORD,  Hon.  William  Eli, 

Senator,  was  b.  in  N.  Y.,  1838.  He 
is  of  Eng.  descent,  though  the 
branch  of  the  family  to  which  he 
belongs  has  been  long  settled  in 
Am.  Losing  his  father  in  early  life, 
he  was  brought  up  and  ed.  by  his 
uncle,  the  late  Edward  Jackson,  of 
Hamilton,  whose  only  dau.  he  after¬ 
wards  married.  He  obtained  his 
early  business  experience  in  N.  Y. 
Subsequently,  he  entered  into  part¬ 
nership  with  Murray  Anderson  and 
Edward  Jackson,  in  London,  Out., 
as  iron  founders.  The  death  of  his 
wife  led  to  his  withdrawal  from  this 
firm.  He  was  afterwards  in  the 
wool  business,  and  was  known  as 
the  “  Wool  King  of  Can.”  In  1861 
the  firm  of  Sanford,  Mclnnes&  Co., 
Hamilton,  engaged  in  the  wholesale 
clothing  trade,  was  founded.  It 
existed  for  10  yrs.  when  Mr.  Mc- 
Innes  withdrew,  and  Mr.  S.  con¬ 
tinued  at  its  head.  This  firm,  it  is 
claimed,  completely  revolutionized 
the  ready-made  clothing  trade  in 
Can.,  giving  to  its  customers  articles 
of  clothing  in  no  way  inferior  in 
quality,  cut  or  finish,  to  the  best 
custom  work.  Only  first-class  work¬ 
men  are  employed,  and  the  best 
of  material  used.  The  firm  has

branches  in  many  places,  employs  a 
cash  capital  of  about  $1,000,000,  and

SAUNDERS,  Miss  Margaret  Mar¬ 
shall,  author,  is  the  dau.  of  the  Rev.

borough  Freeman,  dau.  of  a  W.  I.

1892,  and  “  Beautiful  Joe,”  the 
autobiography  of  a  dog,  with  an 
introductory  note  by  the  Countess 
of  Aberdeen,  in  Philadelphia,  1894. 
The  last-named  work,  which  has 
passed  through  numerous  editions 
and  has  reached  a  circulation  of  over 
200,000,  won  the  $200  prize  offered 
by  the  Am.  Humane  Education  Soc. 
for  the  best  story  illustrative  of  the 
kind  or  cruel  treatment  of  domestic 
animals  and  birds  in  the  northern 
States.  Miss  S.  is  W.  C.  T.  U. 
Supdt.  of  Band  of  Mercy  Work  in 
Halifax,  and  this  book  is  designed 
to  do  for  pet  animals  what  “Black 
Beauty”  has  done  for  the  horse, 
teaching  the  reader  to  look  at  his 
acts  from  the  standpoint  of  the 
dumb  animal.  It  has  been  trans¬ 
lated  into  German  and  Japanese. 
Since  its  publication,  Miss  S.  has 
published:  “Daisy,”  “  Charles  and 
His  Lamb,”  “For  the  Other  Boy’s 
Sake,”  “  The  House  of  Armour,” 
and  “The  King  of  the  Park,”  the 
latter  inculcating  kindness  to  the 
cat  tribe.  Miss  S.  is  a  mem.  of  the 
Bapt.  Ch.  She  lives  much  in  Boston 
but  has  not  ceased  to  be  a  Can. ,  and 
she  believes  emphatically  in  “  Can.

SCADDING,  Rev.  Henry  (Ch.  of 
Eng. ),  author,  is  the  young,  s.  of 
the  late  John  Scadding,  for  many 
yrs.  factor  to  Maj.-Genl.  Simcoe 


(afterwards  Lt.-Gov.  of  U.  C.),  on 
his  estates  in  Devonshire,  Eng.  B. 
at  Dunkeswell,  Devonshire,  Eng., 
July  29,  1813,  he  joined  his  parents 
in  Can.,  1821.  He  received  his  early 
education  at  U.  C.  Coll.,  where 
he  was  “head-boy”  of  the  institu¬ 
tion  in  the  first  year  of  its  existence, 
1830.  In  1833  he  was  apptd.  a 
king’s  scholar,  which  enabled  him  to 
obtain  a  free  course  at  an  Eng. 
univ.  He  proceeded  to  St.  John’s 
Coll.,  Cambridge.  While  there  he 
shared  in  the  influence  resulting 
from  2  movements  which  were  then 
stirring  to  their  depths  the  minds 
of  young  and  old,  viz.,  the  revival 
of  reality  in  ch.  life  and  usage,  con¬ 
sequent  on  a  renewed  exam,  of  ch. 
records  and  documents  anterior  to 
the  division  into  East  and  West  ; 
and  the  Brougham  movement  in  be¬ 
half  of  less  antiquated  methods  of 
education  and  the  diffusion  of  “  use¬ 
ful  knowledge”  among  all  classes. 
Graduating  B.  A.,  1837,  he  returned 
to  Can.,  1838,  to  become  at  once  a 
busy  pioneer  in  the  promotion  of  the 
‘  ‘  new  learning  ”  in  both  its  branches, 
handing  on  the  torch  in  2  capacities : 
1st,  as  a  teacher  of  youth  in  the 
institution  where  he  had  himself 
been  formerly  trained  ;  and  2ndly, 
as  organizer  and  incumbent  of  the 
first  free  ch.  in  Toronto,  the  now 
important  ch.  of  the  Holy  Trinity. 
After  many  yrs.  of  labour  in  these 
2  posts  of  public  usefulness,  he  was 
compelled,  by  a  threatened  break¬ 
down  of  {physical  and  mental  powers, 
to  retire  into  comparative  privacy. 
He  had  proceeded  to  his  M.A. 
degree,  1840.  On  revisiting  Cam¬ 
bridge,  1852,  he  received  the  degree 
ofD.D.  from  his  Alma  Mater,  and,  in 
1867,  he  was  admitted  D.D.  (comi- 
latis  causa),  at  Oxford.  Dr.  S.  was 
for  some  yrs.  ed.  of  the  Joum.  of 
the  Can.  Inst.,  Toronto,  and  while 
occupying  that  position,  and  since, 
contributed  to  its  pages  many  inter¬ 
esting  and  important  papers  on 
philol.,  numismatics  and  Can.  and 
aboriginal  archseol.  His  “Toronto 
of  Old,  or  Collections  and  Recollec¬ 
tions  Illustrative  of  the  Early  Settle-

SCOTT,  Hon.  Richard  William, 
Q.C.,  statesman,  is  the  s.  of  the 
late  W.  J.  Scott,  M.  D. ,  who,  after 
serving  under  Wellington  in  the 
Army  Med.  Dept. ,  came  to  Can.  and 
was  apptd.  Regr.  of  the  Co.  Gren¬ 
ville,  Ont.,  by  his  wife,  Sarah  Ann, 
dau.  of  the  late  Capt.  Allan  Mc¬ 
Donnell,  formerly  an  offr.  in  “The 
King’s  Royal  Yorkers.”  B.  at  Pres¬ 
cott,  Ont.,  Feb.  24,  1825,  he  was  ed. 
there  under  a  private  tutor.  He 
studied  law  in  the  office  of  Crooks 
&  Smith,  Toronto,  and  was  called  to 
the  bar,  1848.  He  entered  on  the 
practice  of  his  profession  in  Ottawa, 
and  soon  became  one  of  the  leaders 
of  the  local  bar.  Elected  Mayor  of 
Ottawa,  1852,  he  was,  at  the  g.  e. 
1857,  returned  to  the  Legislature, 
as  mem.  for  the  city.  After  suffering 


defeat  in  1863,  he  remained  out  of 
public  life  until  the  Union  of  1867, 
when  he  was  elected  to  represent  the 
Federal  Capital  in  the  fii'st  Legisla¬ 
ture  of  Ont.  He  continued  at  To¬ 
ronto  until  1873.  In  Dec.,  1871,  he 
was  elected  Speaker  of  the  Ont. 
Assembly,  and  became  subsequently 
Comnr.  of  Crown  Lands  under  Mr. 
Blake  in  the  Admn.  formed  by  that 
statesman.  He  also  held  the  same 
office  under  Sir  Oliver  Mowat,  who 
succeeded  Mr.  Blake  in  the  premier¬ 
ship  of  Ont.  On  the  formation  of 
the  Mackenzie  Admn.  at  Ottawa, 
Nov.  7,  1873,  he  was  sworn  of  the 
Privy  Council,  and,  in  Jan.,  1874,  he 
was  apptd.  Secy,  of  State  and  Regr.- 
Genl.  of  Can.  He  was  called  to  the 
Senate  by  the  Earl  of  Dufferin,  Mch. 
13,  1874.  Mr.  S.  remained  a  mem. 
of  the  Mackenzie  Govt,  throughout 
its  existence,  retiring  therefrom  with 
his  leader  and  colleagues,  Oct.  16, 
1878.  During  the  whole  of  that 
period  he  was  one  of  the  Govt, 
leaders  in  the  Senate,  becoming 
afterwards  leader  of  the  Opposition 
in  that  body,  conjointly  with  the 
Hon.  Mr.  Pelletier,  C. M.G.  On 
the  formation  of  the  new  Lib.  Cabi¬ 
net  under  Sir  W.  Laurier,  July, 
1896,  he  again  accepted  office  as 
Secy,  of  State  and  Regr.-Genl.  of 
Can.,  and  continues  in  the  same 
at  the  present  time  (1898).  Mr.  S. 
possesses  a  marked  and  ready  adapt¬ 
ability  for  administration,  and  has 
been  called  upon  at  one  time  or  an¬ 
other  during  his  ministerial  career, 
to  discharge  the  duties  of  almost 
every  position  in  the  Cabinet,  the 
duties  being  frequently  cumulative 
in  his  hands.  The  legislative  enact¬ 
ment  by  which  he  is  most  widely 
known,  and  which  it  has  been  said 
forms  his  highest  title  to  a  place 
among  Can.  law-makers,  is  the  Can. 
Temp.  Act,  1875,  otherwise  known  as 
“  The  Scott  Act.”  This  measure 
was  the  outcome  of  a  long  agitation 
on  the  part  of  the  temp,  people  for 
an  advance  in  some  way  upon  the 
license  laws  and  the  old  “  Dunkin 
Act,”  until  then  the  only  ones  in 
force.  The  ‘  ‘  Dunkin  Act  ”  was  a

local  option  measure,  but  was  of  so 
defective  a  character  that  it  was 
but  lightly  considered  by  the  Pro¬ 
hibitionists,  and  was  not  of  much 
use  as  a  guide  in  framing  another 
law  based  upon  the  local  option 
principle.  The  Can.  Temp.  Act, 
therefore,  is  a  pioneer  in  the  path 
of  local  option  legislation  in  regard 
to  the  liquor  traffic,  and  as  a  local 
historian  has  observed,  “it  is  a 
remarkable  tribute  to  the  sagacity 
and  legal  ability  of  its  framer  that 
in  the  22  yrs.  since  it  was  passed, 
although  it  has  been  the  subject  of 
the  fiercest  legal  disputes,  not  only 
has  its  constitutionality  been  upheld 
by  the  highest  court  of  the  Empire, 
in  spite  of  the  determined  efforts  of 
the  greatest  pleaders  to  overthrow 
it,  but  so  perfect  have  its  details 
been  found  that  even  now  some  half 
dozen  amendments  are  all  that  the 
Prohibitionists  are  asking,  and  of 
these  some  arise  out  of  an  advance 
in  the  temp,  sentiment  of  the 
country  which  could  not  have  been 
legislated  for  in  the  first  place.” 
Another  important  Act  which  owes 
its  origin  to  Mr.  S.,  and  which  now 
forms  part  of  our  constitutional  sys¬ 
tem,  is  the  Separate  Sell.  Law  of  Out. , 
prepared  and  carried  through  Parlt. 
by  lam  as  a  private  mem.,  in  1863  ; 
a  measure  which  was  the  means  of 
removing  a  vexed  question  from  the 
political  arena  and  of  allaying  much 
public  irritation.  Both  personally 
and  politically  Mr.  S.  is  exceedingly 
popular  —  in  Toronto  Mr.  Blake 
called  him  “  the  most  popular  mem. 
of  the  House.”  He  entered  politi¬ 
cal  life  as  a  Con. ,  but  since  1871.  has 
been  a  Lib.  In  religion,  ho  is  a  R.C., 
and  has  rendered  important  services 
to  his  Cli.  He  was  for  some  yrs. 
Prosdt.  ofthe  St.  Patrick's  Lit.  Assn.,

SELLAR,  Robert,  author  and  jour¬ 
nalist,  is  a  native  of  Elgin,  Scot. 
He  has  been  for  many  yrs.  ed.  and 
prop,  of  the  Can.  Gleaner  (Hunting¬ 
don,  P.Q.).  In  this  paper  was  first 
published  the  stories  written  by 
him,  known  as  the  “  Gleaner  Tales,” 
which  have  since  appeared  in  book- 
fornt  (2nd  ed.,  1895).  Some  of  these 
tales  are  based  on  actual  incidents 
in  the  lives  of  the  early  settlers  in 
the  old  Co.  of  Huntingdon,  and  the 
scenes  of  all  are  laid  in  the  wedge- 
shaped  territory  which  forms  the 
south-western  extremity  of  the  Pro¬ 
vince  of  Quebec,  with  the  St.  Law¬ 
rence  on  one  side  and  the  U.  S.  on 
the  other.  They  display  a  high  de¬ 
gree  of  literary  merit.  Indeed,  it 
has  been  said  of  some  of  them,  that 
no  Can.  writer  surpasses  Mr.  S.  in 
his  charm  of  narrative  and  delicacy 


of  style.  Later,  he  published 
“  Hemlock  :  a  Tale  of  the  War  of 
1812,”  which  is  also  a  contribution 
to  the  semi-historical  literature  of 
Can.  Mr.  S.  is  likewise  the  author 
of  “The  History  of  the  Co.  of 
Huntingdon  and  of  the  Seigniories 
of  Chateauguay  and  Beauharnois 
from  their  First  Settlement  to  the 
year  1838  ”  (1888).  As  a  journalist, 
Mr.  S.  has  been  for  several  yrs.  the 
accepted  interpreter  of  the  feelings 
and  aspirations  of  the  Prot.  minority 
in  Quebec.  He  was  the  author  of 
the  pamphlet  signed  ‘  ‘  Quebec  Loy- 
alist,”  describing  “  The  Disabilities 
of  Protestants  in  the  Province  of 
Quebec,”  which  was  published  by  the 
Equal  Rights  Assn,  of  Ont. ,  during 
the  agitation  raised  by  Mr.  Mercier’s 
Jesuits’  Estates  Bill,  1888 ;  of  a  letter 
addressed  to  Sir  H.  G.  Joly,  “In 
Defence  of  the  Quebec  Minority  ” 
(Feb.,  1894),  and  of  various  papers 
communicated  to  the  Toronto  Globe 
and  other  journals  in  reference  to 
the  Man.  Sch.  question.  As  a  lec¬ 
turer  he  has  won  more  than  a  local 
reputation,  one  of  the  best  of  his 
efforts  in  this  line  being  “  The 
Scottish  Pioneers  of  Can.”  Politi¬ 
cally,  a  Lib. ;  in  religious  faith,  he 
is  a  Presb.  He  m.  the  dau.  of  the 
Rev.  Dr.  Watson  (Presb.). — Hunt¬ 
ingdon,  P.  Q.
